6ab4ca5362a47b6beca89783.one_liner: A broad-strokes HSBC macro podcast on Fed tightening and how Asian central banks (especially Japan, and by contrast mainland China) are responding, with a direct read-through to the HKD peg and HK rate sensitivity.
6ab4ca5362a47b6beca89783.recap: HSBC's Harald van der Linde and Fred Neumann discuss the Fed's latest hike, framed as hawkish given persistent inflation from rising energy (diesel) prices and a brewing El Niño threatening Asian food inflation. Markets are pricing further hikes since the Fed historically moves in multi-step cycles rather than one-off adjustments. Because the Fed sets the global price of money, most Asian central banks are following suit to avoid currency weakness feeding import-cost inflation: Japan's central bank hiked days after the Fed (unusual after decades of near-zero rates, driven by rising wages and food prices), with Australia, Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines and India also expected to tighten. Mainland China is the outlier, with disinflation/near-deflation and weak consumption/investment giving its central bank room to hold or even ease; capital controls insulate the renminbi from the usual divergence-driven outflow pressure, and HSBC's house view sees room for RMB strength on export surpluses. On equities, rising rates should pressure valuations, but AI-driven capex is generating order flow for Asian tech supply chains, complicating the picture. Hong Kong, due to its USD currency peg, is described as unusually rate-sensitive, and the hosts note a Hong Kong-versus-Shanghai listing arbitrage where the same mainland company can be priced differently due to capital-flow differences. The episode closes with a lighthearted forecast game: hosts predict India, Korea, Indonesia and Taiwan raise rates over six months, while China stays on hold.
